aspects.appliesWhen: The code under test computes an anniversary, an age, or a yearly recurrence, so February 29 exists in a leap year and does not in a common year.

The code under test computes a monthly recurrence, a due date, or a period that can land in a month shorter than the chosen day-of-month, so the 31st, 30th, 29th and 28th cases each behave differently.
The code under test buckets rows by period, or compares a period against the previous one, so the first and last day of the period and the seam between periods each decide a boundary.
The code under test converts a wall-clock date, or stores a date submitted in local time, so an instant in the small hours can resolve to the wrong local day.
The code under test writes to the database and the test asserts what was written, not only what was returned.
One domain event reaches more than one delivery channel, so the email, the pushed payload and the persisted notification row must agree with each other.
The handler under test can receive event metadata that violates its schema, so it must log and continue rather than throw and abort the bus.
Delivery of a notification depends on per-user event preferences, so each preference combination changes what is delivered.
The code under test decides which users receive a notification, so the correct recipients and the deliberately excluded ones are both part of the contract.
The code under test reads or writes a table that carries a Postgres row-level-security policy, or the test asserts the policy itself.
The code under test deletes, archives, closes or otherwise retires a record that the schema retires by flag rather than by row removal.
The code under test returns rows that reach a real client-facing surface, so synthetic or demo client organisations must not appear in the result.

rules.statement: A test asserts a returned object whole, in one toEqual against a hand-computed expected value. It does not pick the object apart field by field.
rules.rationale: Field-by-field assertions pin only the fields the author already thought about. A field the code stops returning, a field it starts returning, or a wrong value in any field nobody named all pass. This is not theoretical in this repository: on PR #3024 the author changed production business logic three times - stored 0 instead of the paid amount, never auto-disbursed, and handed the four-eyes review to its own creator - and the suite stayed green fourteen times out of fourteen. His diagnosis was the shape of the assertions: 'we only assert the fields we read, so the rest of the business logic is free to change underneath us.' A single whole-object toEqual against a hand-computed expected value fails on all three.
rules.archaeology: OVERRIDE, and the largest conformance gap in the codex. The assertions aspect carries a NEAR-TOTAL bar, whose stated meaning is that the pattern must hold in nearly every applicable file or the aspect ships no rule at all. Measured conformance is 39 of 151 files that assert a returned subject, 25.8%; 102 files assert field-by-field with no whole comparison and 10 do both. Captain Lasky adopted it blocking on 2026-08-09 as an explicit override, having been shown the bar, the figure and the seed taxonomy's own warning that a loose near-total bar 'invents house rules nobody agreed to and burns the human's trust on noise'. It also OVERRIDES a written repository document: agent-os/specs/dashboard/2026-04-07-dashboard-widget-integration-tests/implementation/integration-test-conventions.md section 5.4 requires concrete values rather than shapes but demonstrates four separate expects on one object in its own Invariants block. Captain Lasky ruled that document must be updated to match this rule. The corpus-level history is accident at medium confidence: structural assertion entered with the first toEqual in the repository, aa60b78ac (2024-10-22), as Vitest default vocabulary, and 109 of the 162 files that assert no structural shape were created in a single 2025-10/11 coverage sprint by three authors - the correlate is the calendar, not a decision. The one decided, argued and codified instance is the recorder-transcript rule, whose scope this rule deliberately extends beyond.

appliesWhen.human: The test file inspects a returned subject - a value bound as result, data, returned or response - as an object: it reads a field of the subject inside an expect, passes the subject through a named helper inside an expect, or compares the bare subject against an object or array literal. A file whose only subject assertion is a scalar comparison, such as expect(result).toBe("a-string"), asserts no returned OBJECT and is not applicable. DTO and schema validation tests are excluded by path.

detect.human: Collect every assertion made on the returned subject: each field-level access inside an expect, each named helper wrapping the subject inside an expect, and each whole-object toEqual on the subject itself, with line numbers. Return the sites, no verdict.

violates.human: Violation when the file inspects a returned subject field by field and never compares that subject whole with toEqual. A single toEqual on the subject passes. A named call wrapping the subject is still the subject: expect(extractTotalClaimStatus(result)).toEqual(...) is a whole-object comparison of the projected subject and passes. An inline projection written at the assertion site - expect(result.rows.map((r) => r.id)).toEqual(...) - is a field-level assertion and does not pass. toBeCloseTo on a derived floating-point value is a sanctioned exception for that field, not a licence to skip the whole-object comparison.

rubric.expects: The fields actually asserted, against the fields the subject returns.

rubric.expects: The toBeCloseTo line and the whole-object comparison, or a statement that none exists.

rubric.question: Where the subject is wrapped in a named helper, does that helper return the whole subject or only a narrow projection of it?
rubric.expects: The helper body, and a statement of whether the comparison is still a whole-object one.

rules.statement: A test that drives work finishing after the call returns waits on a condition, never on a fixed duration. It awaits waitForBusIdle(container) for the bus, or a NAMED polling helper the sink provides such as waitForEmails or waitForNotification. A hand-rolled deadline loop that sleeps between checks is not such a helper and does not qualify. Tests whose subject IS the bus transport are out of scope, because there the delay is the behaviour under test.
rules.rationale: A fixed sleep is a bet that the handler finishes inside that window on the slowest machine that will ever run the suite. When it does, the test passes without proving the handler ran; when it does not, the suite fails intermittently and the failure never reproduces alone. PURCO-3050 measured the first half directly: 182 injected code changes were swept and 17 real coverage gaps closed, including async-event gaps that only a real event-bus drain plus notification-row assertions could catch. The second half is the 19 half-second sleeps in exported-claims.handler.test.ts, which cost the suite roughly ten seconds of wall time per run and still prove nothing about ordering.
rules.archaeology: waitForBusIdle is deliberate, high confidence. Introduced in 2a06b07e5 (2026-05-19) as a 29-line helper, tests/integration/utils/communications-bus-idle.ts, created inside the PURCO-2976 payment-attribution commit whose body never mentions it; PR #3013 shows no argument about the shape. The intent is recorded in two later places. First, the helper corrects a written and dated FALSE assumption: the PURCO-2938 test plan at test-plan.md:50 (2026-05-06, thirteen days earlier) states 'Event bus runs synchronously inside the test process; handlers fire inline. Assertions run after execute() resolves', which the helper's own depth-polling guard disproves. Second, PURCO-3050 (d215a7fed, PR #3029) supplies the measured consequence quoted in the rationale. It was codified at .claude/rules/testing-backend.md:73 by 25215eb94 (2026-07-16) by the same author who created it. Taught, not copied: adopted across four unrelated domains by three authors within two months. No reversal - 311 lines added against 28 removed, every removal a file rebuild. The arbitrary-wait shape is accident, high confidence: no commit, review thread or ticket ever mentions a wait, a race or a timing problem, and no reviewer objected to a sleep on PRs #2504, #3003, #3029 or #2999. The newest sleep landed 13 days AFTER the drain rule was written down. IMPORTANT: the clause 'never spy on the publisher' is NOT part of this rule and was never stated anywhere - the PURCO-2938 spec MANDATES a publisher spy at lines 400, 428, 441, 453 and 529. VERSION 2 (2026-08-09): statement narrowed, appliesWhen widened, violates clarified; every fixture label is unchanged. Version 1 failed its blind acceptance gate at 3 of 5, twice, with two independent Inspectors returning identical verdicts and missing the SAME two files. First, appliesWhen matched only setTimeout immediately followed by resolve, so scrive.service.test.ts was never governed at all: its setTimeout calls at lines 928, 959 and 988 schedule a callback inside a stub and take an arrow function, not resolve. That file is labelled follows precisely because it carries the surface mark without carrying the fault, so a rule that cannot even reach it can never award it the pass its label requires; both Inspectors reported finding no wait site and scored it not-applicable. Second, version 1's carve-out for the sink's polling helper was open enough that both Inspectors read a hand-rolled while loop over Date.now() with a 50ms sleep as sanctioned, and passed stripe.webhook.handler.test.ts, which is labelled violates because the sleep is residue sitting beside nine correct waitForBusIdle drains. Version 2 restricts the carve-out to a named sink helper and states outright that a correct barrier elsewhere in the file does not excuse a sleep.

appliesWhen.human: The test file waits for work it does not control - it sleeps on a fixed duration, or awaits a drain or polling helper. Tests whose subject is the bus transport itself are excluded by path: there the fixed delay is the behaviour being asserted, not a wait for someone else's work. Any setTimeout in the file makes it applicable, including one that merely schedules a callback inside a stub, because separating that use from a wait the test awaits is exactly what the rubric decides.

violates.human: Violation when the file waits on a fixed duration - a promise wrapping setTimeout, or an awaited local sleep helper. Awaiting waitForBusIdle or a polling helper is a condition wait and passes. A setTimeout used to schedule a callback inside a stub or fake, rather than to wait, is not a violation. A sleep is still a violation when a correct barrier exists elsewhere in the file; residue beside a correct drain is the case this rule most often has to catch. A setTimeout used inside a bounded while loop that polls for a condition is a hand-rolled wait, not a sanctioned polling helper, and is a violation.

rules.statement: A test that triggers an email asserts the delivered message itself - its exact subject, and concrete content from its body. Asserting only that a message arrived is not enough.
rules.rationale: The repository stopped mocking mail precisely so the real message could be inspected: the subject line, the rendered template, and the values interpolated into it all run for real against the Maildev container. A test that only counts delivered messages throws that away - it proves the send fired, and nothing about who it addressed, what it said, or which amount it quoted. Every email defect that reaches a customer is a content defect: a wrong amount, a wrong date, a blank sender, a template that rendered an empty variable. Counting messages cannot catch any of them.

The rule's ceiling is 5 of 6 by construction, not by defect. VERSION 3 (2026-08-10): the checks were nevertheless rewritten from raw text onto the AST vocabulary, identically to the re-issue, so that whichever rule the human keeps carries the corrected mechanism. appliesWhen now follows an imported assert-helper one level and asks whether its body calls waitForEmails, which is how a file that inspects the message through assertNotificationDispatched is governed at all; violates now requires the word subject to appear as a property key or a property read in executable code. rules.statement: A test that intercepts Pusher asserts what was actually sent - the channel, the event name, or the payload - or asserts the downstream artefact the push produced. Installing the interceptor without asserting on it proves nothing.
rules.rationale: The interceptor exists so the real pusher.service.ts runs end to end and its HTTP call can be inspected. A test that installs MSW and never reads the captured request has paid the whole cost of the wire boundary and collected none of the benefit: the channel could be wrong, the event name could be misspelled, the payload could be empty, and the test still passes. This is the same failure the whole-array recorder rule prevents on the database side, on the other outbound edge.
rules.archaeology: OVERRIDE, recorded as such: conformance is 4 of 41 files, 9.8%, far below the majority bar. Captain Lasky adopted it blocking on 2026-08-09 having been shown that figure. The interception layer itself is deliberate at high confidence and decided in writing: agent-os/specs/split-notifications-and-improvements/2026-05-06-unified-notifications-redesign/testing/test-plan.md:54 states 'Do NOT mock IPusherService or vi.mock("pusher"). Let pusher.service.ts run end-to-end. The Pusher SDK v5 uses node-fetch internally and makes real fetch() calls ... Intercept those HTTP calls using MSW', and line 206 repeats it as 'MSW intercept - no mocks'. tests/integration/utils/pusher-msw.ts was created in a1aa454a5 (2026-05-07) alongside that spec. What the spec never states is what must be asserted about the intercepted request, which is why 41 files intercept and only 4 read the capture. IMPORTANT: the same spec MANDATES a publisher spy at lines 400, 428, 441, 453 and 529, so this rule must never be read as banning spies - it requires an assertion on the delivered artefact, whether that is the captured request or the notification row the push produced. VERSION 2 (2026-08-10): the check was rewritten from raw-text regex onto the AST vocabulary and given helper resolution. The v1 check keyed on the bare token userNotification, which passed any file that merely cleaned up user-notification rows, and it could not see an assertion written inside an imported helper. Nine handler suites that assert the capture inside assertNotificationDispatched were mis-scored as violators by v1 and pass under v2. NOTE FOR THE HUMAN: under v2 the labelled violator create-payment-allocations.usecase.test.ts reads follows, because it asserts the persisted notification row through waitForNotification - the same proof for which its sibling fixture create-recurring-payment.usecase.test.ts is labelled follows. The two labels are in tension and one of them needs a decision.

appliesWhen.human: The test file installs the Pusher MSW interceptor. A file that does not intercept Pusher is not applicable.

violates.human: Violation when the file intercepts Pusher and asserts neither the captured request nor the downstream artefact the push produced. Asserting a persisted notification row instead of the raw request is a pass: the artefact arrived, which is what the boundary exists to prove. The assertion counts wherever it is written: reading pusher.requests directly, reading the notification row directly, or calling an imported assert/expect/wait helper whose body does either, are all the same proof.

rules.statement: A test of a read or query path asserts against a data population it controls: rows it created, or a named seed fixture module whose expected values are derived from that module. When the edge case a query needs is not present in the seed, the seed is extended rather than the assertion weakened.
rules.rationale: A query is only as tested as the population it runs against. A test that asserts on whatever the ambient seed happens to hold proves the query returns something, not that it returns the right thing at a boundary - and the boundaries are where query defects live: an empty result, a single row, a tie, a row on the period edge, a row belonging to another organisation. Extending the seed with the missing case makes that boundary permanent and shared; weakening the assertion to fit the seed makes the gap invisible. PURCO-3160 is the model: it added bucket-report-data.ts (2,982 lines), bucket-report-seed-rows.ts (478) and bucket-report-expectations.ts (511) alongside a 1,091-line test, so the report's expected values are derived from a declared population rather than observed from an ambient one.

Palmer checked the claim and it is corroborated by the commit record - PURCO-3056 (07b5f322e) added roughly 65,000 lines of seed data across twelve seed files, and PURCO-3160 (c397c9831) added a named seed module, a seed-rows module and an expectations module alongside its test. rules.statement: EACH discriminating claim a read-path test makes - a filter, a sort, a pagination bound, an exclusion - must run against a population containing at least one row that claim has to REJECT. The rule is judged per claim: one claim whose population cannot discriminate is a violation, however many sound claims sit beside it.
rules.rationale: A list endpoint that returns one row, tested against a population of one row, cannot fail. The assertion shapes that read as thorough are the ones that go vacuous first: result.items.forEach and result.every both pass on an empty array; comparing result.count to a mirror Prisma query that repeats the same predicate is satisfied by 0 === 0 and moves in lockstep when the predicate is deleted from the usecase; toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0) is true for every possible result; and a silent return or testCtx.skip() reports green having asserted nothing. What makes such a test worse than no test is that it names the behaviour it fails to check, so the coverage gap is invisible on inspection. The remedy is a population with a near-miss in it: a row one day outside the date range, a non-matching status inside it, a soft-deleted row, an archived claim's row, another organisation's row.
rules.archaeology: Drafted 2026-08-09 from a sweep of 147 read-path backend test files, of which 107 assert on a collection. The rule replaces backend-data-setup-query-population-controlled, which was retired on the mistaken ground that it duplicated backend-isolation-test-creates-its-own-subject. It does not: that rule governs data OWNERSHIP, and this one governs population RICHNESS, and a test can own every row it reads while still holding only rows its filter keeps. The distinction was supplied by the engineer who requested the rule: for get endpoints a large varied dataset is seeded so that filtering can be exercised properly. The corpus supports both routes. appliesWhen.human: The test file resolves a read usecase from the container - a name beginning Get, List, Export or Search, or ending Report or Query - AND asserts a discriminating behaviour on the result: a filter, a sort order, pagination, or an exclusion. A read test that asserts only a single-row happy path, a schema shape, or an authorisation refusal is not governed; the rule polices discrimination claims, not every read. detect.human: Collect, without judging: every row-creating call before the query, with its model and the field values that differ between calls; every named seed module import; every assertion on the result, marking which are loops over the returned rows and which pin an identifier, a count or an ordered array; and every vacuous shape - toBeGreaterThanOrEqual, a comparison against a mirror Prisma query, a bare return, a testCtx.skip().

violates.human: Violation when the file asserts a discriminating behaviour against a population that cannot discriminate. Ask what would happen if the behaviour were deleted from the usecase: if the assertion still holds, it is a violation. Concretely: no row is present that the filter must reject; or every assertion about the filtered set is a loop over the returned rows, which passes on an empty result; or the expected count is a mirror query carrying the same predicate; or the deciding assertion is toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0). Richness obtained by SELECTION rather than seeding passes, provided the test proves the selected population discriminates - asserting the candidate count is above zero, or that a non-matching row exists. Assuming the ambient seed discriminates does not pass. Judge each claim separately and report the weakest. A file passes only when EVERY discriminating claim it makes has a rejectable row present. Adaptive expectations that scale to whatever the population happens to hold - Math.min, a ternary on the candidate count, a distinctness check gated inside an if - are the signature of a claim that cannot discriminate, because they cannot fail.

rules.statement: A test file that persists the same entity shape three or more times extracts that seeding into a named helper declared at file or describe scope, never inline inside each test, taking the data client as its first parameter. A file that declares at least one such helper passes even while some inline persistence remains; the rule asks whether extraction happened, not whether it is complete.
rules.rationale: Seeding repeated inline is the schema contract copied once per test. A new required column then breaks every copy separately, and each is fixed separately in the same file. A named helper also makes the seeded shape readable at a glance and lets a test state only what differs from the default, which is what makes a hand-computed expected value checkable. The convention is already specified precisely enough to follow without judgement.
rules.archaeology: OVERRIDE, and a direction rather than a description: only about 60 of 408 files declare any top-level async helper, 15 declare a seed helper and 12 declare a lookup helper. Captain Lasky adopted it advisory on 2026-08-09 knowing that figure. The convention itself is written down in unusual detail at agent-os/specs/dashboard/2026-04-07-dashboard-widget-integration-tests/implementation/integration-test-conventions.md sections 2.1 and 2.5, derived there from the file the document calls the gold standard, get-client-communication-log.usecase.test.ts. Section 2.1 specifies the signature exactly - a top-level async function, not a const arrow function; first parameter always db: PrismaService; remaining parameters a named object rather than positional arguments; createMany for bulk creation; returns void. Section 2.5 adds the lookup-helper form. No commit, review thread or ticket argues the convention; it exists only in that document, which is why this is an override rather than a corpus reading. VERSION 2 (2026-08-09) relaxed the statement and widened both checks after a 3-of-5 blind gate. VERSION 3 (2026-08-09) added a counting threshold and a partial-extraction allowance. VERSION 4 (2026-08-10): the checks were rewritten from raw text onto the AST vocabulary, and a REAL BUG was fixed. The v3 violates regex was ast:none(rawText(/^\s*(async function |const \w+\s*=\s*(async\s*)?\()/)) with no multiline flag, so the ^ anchored at offset zero of the file and the pattern could match nothing but the first line: the check flagged 270 of 422 backend files, including three of its own four labelled followers, and scored 2 of 5 against its own fixtures. v4 matches a declaration at the start of any line. NOTE FOR THE HUMAN: with the bug fixed, the labelled violator billing-account.repository.test.ts reads follows, because it declares makeClaimWithClient at describe scope and calls it six times. That is exactly the escape the rule's own statement grants - 'a file that declares at least one named seeding or lookup helper passes, even if the helper covers only some of the repeated shapes'. Either the statement or that label needs a decision; the check now follows the statement.

rules.statement: A test that pins a February date for a subject that derives a yearly recurrence, an age, an anniversary or a days-in-month value pins February 29 of a leap year and a February date of a common year. One February is not a boundary.
rules.rationale: February is the only month whose length changes, so a subject that reasons about February at all has two behaviours and a test pinning one February exercises one of them. The failure is silent and annual: a yearly recurrence set on February 29 has no February 29 in three out of four years, and a days-in-month computation pinned to a 28-day February never sees 29. Leap years in range for this codebase are 2024, 2028, 2032 and 2040.
rules.archaeology: Drafted 2026-08-09. 28 backend test files pin a February date. Three finish the boundary: process-saved-report-fire.test.ts pins 2028-02-29 at 1861 against 2027-02-28 at 1941 and names leap at 1842 and 1922; saved-report-lifecycle.workflow.test.ts pins 2028-02-29 at 108-109 and 2029-02-28 at 118-119; get-previous-period-range.test.ts pins leap 2024-02-29 at 219 against common 2026-02-28 at 132, 193 and 206. Three do not: compute-preliminary-cash-periods.test.ts asserts a February daysInMonth at 81-90 while pinning only 2026-02-28 at 35 and 77, and its own title names dayOfMonth and daysInMonth for February; get-claim-stats.usecase.test.ts pins every February literal inside leap 2040 at 239-252 and none on the 28th or 29th while asserting previous-period comparisons; process-scheduled-late-fees.test.ts walks a monthly late fee across February pinned only in non-leap 2026 at 1375-1376. VERSION 2 (2026-08-10): the checks were rewritten from raw text onto the AST vocabulary and the DERIVATION GATE was added to violates. February literals are now read out of call arguments rather than from raw file text, so a February date inside a comment no longer governs a file; and a file is only a violator when the derivation is visible in it - a leap or days-in-month title, or a days-in-month, leap-year or add-years computation. rules.statement: A test that pins a day-of-month of 28 or later, for a subject that derives a monthly recurrence, due date or period end, also pins the 28-day February case. Pinning only the 31st proves nothing about what happens when the month is shorter.
rules.rationale: A monthly due date on the 31st has no 31st in February, and the code must choose: clamp to the last day, roll forward, or skip. A test that only ever pins the 31st exercises one of those three and cannot distinguish them, so the wrong choice ships. The 28th is the universal counterpart because every month has one, which makes it the cheapest possible proof that the short-month path was considered at all. This is not hypothetical in this codebase: monthly recurrence drives payment plans, promissory notes, recurring payments, saved-report cron schedules and late-fee walks, and the day-of-month is user-chosen in each.
rules.archaeology: Drafted 2026-08-09 from a sweep of the backend corpus. 42 files pin a day-of-month of 28 or later; an earlier count of this class reported 0 because the regex required an ISO T separator and therefore missed every plain "2025-01-31" literal, which made month length look like a non-issue when it is the largest date class in the corpus. rules.statement: A test that asserts a period filter or a previous-period comparison pins a row just OUTSIDE the period as well as rows inside it. An existence-only assertion over inside-rows cannot detect a one-day slip in the range.
rules.rationale: A period range has two edges and each is exclusive or inclusive. A test seeding only rows inside the range cannot tell a correct boundary from one that is a day wide, and an assertion of the form toHaveProperty holds regardless of which rows came back. This is not theoretical: PURCO-3101 was a quarter double-count caused by getPreviousPeriodRange producing a previous-period end that overlapped the current period start, and it survived because no test bracketed the seam.
rules.archaeology: Drafted 2026-08-09 from a sweep of 82 backend test files pinning a quarter-end or period-first-day literal or referencing DashboardPeriod. Three finish the boundary: get-previous-period-range.test.ts asserts at 333-341 that THIS_QUARTER over 2026-04-01 to 2026-06-30 clamps previousPeriodEnd to the day before periodStart, which is the PURCO-3101 seam directly; recovery-performance.usecase.test.ts brackets a 2025-01-01 to 2025-01-31 CUSTOM period with rows at 2024-12-31 and 2025-02-01 at 647-658; get-top-performing-claims.usecase.test.ts pins 2026-04-01 against 2026-03-31, 2026-01-01 against 2025-12-31 and 2025-03-31 against 2025-04-01 at 1569-1603 with previous-period assertions. Three do not: get-capped-revenue-stats.usecase.test.ts walks three back-to-back exact calendar quarters at 165-206 with every row inside and every assertion a toHaveProperty, so previousAmount exclusivity is never proven; claim-count.usecase.test.ts uses wide inside-only ranges at 100-101, 161-162 and 482-483 with no row a day outside; get-client-communication-log.usecase.test.ts filters to a 2025-06-30 quarter end at 249 with inside rows only.

It is also a violation when every seeded row falls inside the period, leaving no row the boundary must exclude. A file passes when it pins a row a day outside the range, or asserts the exact clamped boundary value. A file whose period reference is only a shape assertion with no rows seeded is not governed rather than violating.

rules.statement: A test that names a timezone or pins a small-hours UTC instant pins instants on BOTH sides of the local-day boundary. One instant proves nothing, because a wrong offset moves every instant the same way.
rules.rationale: Denver is UTC-7 in summer and UTC-6 in winter, so an instant at 00:00Z is the previous evening locally. A test pinning only 00:00Z cannot distinguish a correct conversion from an offset applied in the wrong direction, or from no conversion at all - every one of those yields the same single answer. The boundary is only proven when two instants that straddle the local midnight are pinned and land on different local days. This has produced real defects here: dates submitted late in the evening were stored against the following day.
rules.archaeology: Drafted 2026-08-09 from a sweep of 72 backend test files that name a timezone or pin a T00 to T06 instant. Three finish the boundary: financial-summary.usecase.test.ts pins an included instant at 4137-4205 and an excluded one at 4205-4241 and asserts MST/MDT parity at 4449; client-communication.usecase.test.ts pins 2025-07-01T06:00:00.001Z as outside at 768 against 2025-06-30T23:59:59.999Z and a 23:45Z instant as inside at 980-983 and 687; preliminary-cash.usecase.test.ts freezes 05:00Z at 1703 then counts a 2025-06-14T22:00Z instant at 1720 and excludes a 2025-06-15T10:00Z one at 1732. Three do not: statute.repository.test.ts pins 2025-12-17T00:00:00Z at 37 while its own comment documents the 9 PM Denver case as 04:00Z the following day, so the instant pinned is 17:00 Denver and the boundary the test names is never exercised; client-health.usecase.test.ts pins 25 instants all at T00:00:00.000Z at 4018-4060 and names Denver only in a comment; promissory-note.service.test.ts pins a single Denver late-night instant at 353-377 with no daytime counterpart, so a half-day offset error still passes.

appliesWhen.human: The test file names a timezone in executable code or in a test title - America/, Denver, Mountain, MST or MDT - or constructs a UTC instant in the small hours, T00 through T06, through Date or a Denver instant helper. A file doing neither is not governed. A timezone named only inside a comment does not govern the file.

detect.human: Collect every pinned UTC instant with its hour and line; every named timezone with its line; and every assertion that a row is included in or excluded from a day, a range or a bucket. Note which instants fall in the small hours and which fall in local daytime.

violates.human: Violation when the file pins only small-hours instants, or only one instant, for a subject that buckets by local day - so a wrong or absent offset would not change any assertion. The daytime counterpart may be pinned through a helper: denverInstant(day, "22:00:00") and anchorDenverClock(day, "14:00:00") pin the far side of the Denver day exactly as a T22 literal would. A file passes when it pins instants on both sides of a local-day boundary, or asserts MST and MDT parity. A file also passes when it names no local-day semantics at all - no timezone, no Denver helper - because then the instant is incidental, feeding a hash or an identifier.

rubric.expects: The instants with line numbers, marked small-hours or daytime.

rubric.question: Does the subject convert a wall-clock date or bucket by local day, or is the instant incidental to it?
rubric.expects: The converting line in the production code, or a statement that the instant carries no local-day semantics.

rubric.question: If the offset were applied in the wrong direction, or not at all, would any assertion here fail?
rubric.expects: The discriminating assertion, or a statement that none exists.

rubric.question: Where the daytime counterpart is pinned through a helper, does the helper argument really land on the far side of the local day?
rubric.expects: The helper call with its wall-time argument, and the local day it resolves to.

rules.statement: A test that records effects asserts each recorded array whole, in one toEqual. Neither the mutations array nor the stripeCalls array is ever the subject of a filter, a some, a find, a length or a count - not even alongside a whole-array comparison.
rules.rationale: A count, a length or a partial match on one element pins only what the author already expected. An unexpected extra write, a missing write, or a wrong field in an unnamed position all pass. This is not hypothetical: on PR #3024 the author changed production business logic three times - stored 0 instead of the paid amount, never auto-disbursed, and handed the four-eyes review to its own creator - and the suite stayed green fourteen times out of fourteen. His diagnosis was the shape of the assertions: 'we only assert the fields we read, so the rest of the business logic is free to change underneath us.' The same reasoning applies with more force to stripeCalls, because an unasserted extra Stripe call is a second charge against a customer's card rather than a stray database row.
rules.archaeology: Written verbatim in this repository at .claude/rules/testing-backend.md:75-119 by 26898d663 (PR #3086, PURCO-3109, committed 2026-07-22): 'assert the entire ordered array in one toEqual, never a filtered subset ... never reach for .filter(...), .some(...), .find(...), or a count as a substitute.' The harness was born at the Stripe boundary in d215a7fed (PURCO-3050, PR #3029, 2026-06-21) and split into effect-recorders/ three days later by d7af1754c (PURCO-3044). CORRECTING AN EARLIER HYPOTHESIS: PURCO-3044 is NOT a bug about an unverified database write - it is '[BUG] Late Fee addition not working correctly when setting up recurring payments', and the unchecked 'history' is the domain payment history used for late-fee computation. It must not be cited as this aspect's rationale. Archivist verdict deliberate, high confidence: 49 files, three authors, unrelated features, monotone, no reversal. VERSION 1 (2026-08-09): Captain Lasky chose the strict form, flagging a subset assertion even alongside a correct whole-array compare, because a reader cannot tell an additional proof from a substitute. VERSION 2 (2026-08-09): scope corrected to cover stripeCalls, which line 95 of the written rule always required and version 1 had omitted - 10 files read stripeCalls and all 10 already assert it whole, 3 of them also subset it. Deliberately NOT generalised to emails or pusher.requests, which were never measured. VERSION 3 (2026-08-09): detect corrected. Versions 1 and 2 used ast:count(rawText(/.../)) >= 0, true for every file and returning an empty sites array; every Inspector in the tenancy gate independently reported the shape carries no information. Doctrine requires detect to COLLECT sites without judging, and a boolean comparison collects nothing. Replaced with a plain grep over the same identifiers.

rules.statement: A test names a feature flag through the FEATURE_FLAGS constant. It never keys a flag by a raw string literal, including inside a hand-rolled flags stub.
rules.rationale: A flag keyed by a literal is invisible to the type system. FeatureFlagKey is a string-literal union derived from FEATURE_FLAGS, so a reference to the constant fails type checking the moment a flag is renamed or removed, while a raw literal keeps compiling and the test keeps asserting a flag that no longer exists. The single corpus violator hides its literal inside a hand-rolled stub - isFeatureEnabled: (key) => key === 'enable_claim_exports_columns_split_for_pd_lou_and_af' - which is exactly where the type never reaches. That test would go on passing against a renamed flag while the production path it claims to cover no longer runs.
rules.archaeology: The FEATURE_FLAGS constant was created in 20d4ed280 (2025-07-10) inside PURCO-2406, a letter-templates feature, with no stated decision about keying. The convention was then unanimous for about twelve months with no enforcement beyond the FeatureFlagKey type, which constrains a flag to a valid value but still admits a correct string literal. It was ratified twice, both after the fact: in writing by 25215eb94 (2026-07-16, CLAUDE.md, 'Always key flags with the FEATURE_FLAGS constant ... never magic strings'), and mechanically by 5db4f2338 and 6c794de73 (2026-08-03), which added the local no-magic-enum-strings lint rule whose registry parses src/types/feature-flags.ts explicitly. That lint rule is set to 'warn', not 'error', and it landed six days before this survey, so it recorded the convention and cannot have caused it. Archivist verdict deliberate, high confidence. Correction to Palmer's Stage 1 census: the flagStringLiteral column reported 0 violations; the true count is 1. VERSION 2 (2026-08-09): detect corrected only. Version 1 used ast:count(rawText(/.../)) >= 0, which is true for every file and returns an empty sites array; every Inspector in the tenancy acceptance gate independently reported the shape carries no information. Doctrine requires detect to COLLECT sites without judging, and a boolean comparison collects nothing. Replaced with a plain grep over the same tokens.

detect.human: Collect every site where a flag key is named: a member access on FEATURE_FLAGS, a comparison against a flag-shaped string literal inside an isFeatureEnabled implementation, and any computed object key that is a flag-shaped string literal mapped to a boolean. Return the sites with line numbers, no verdict.

violates.human: Violation when a flag-shaped string literal is used as the key by which a flag is looked up or compared - inside an isFeatureEnabled implementation, as an argument to isFeatureEnabled, or as a computed object key mapped to a boolean. Asserting that a FEATURE_FLAGS member equals its literal value is NOT a violation: there the literal is the value under test, not the key.

rubric.expects: The line, and whether the literal appears on the left of a lookup or on the right of an equality assertion whose left side is a FEATURE_FLAGS member.

rules.statement: A test never replaces a provider transport module with vi.mock when the repository already owns an interception layer for that provider. Pusher is intercepted with pusher-msw, mail with the Maildev container, Stripe with the effect recorder, and storage and the scheduler by the shared setup's container rebinds. vi.mock is reserved for modules the test process cannot reach.
rules.rationale: Replacing the transport module unexecutes every line between the call site and the wire. The subject's own client construction, request serialisation, header and signature assembly, and provider-error mapping all stop running, so a change to the request the subject builds cannot fail the test, and the double drifts away from the provider with no signal. Intercepting at the wire instead leaves that code running and asserts the artefact that actually arrived. The written decision states the mechanism directly: let pusher.service.ts run end to end and intercept its HTTP calls.
rules.archaeology: Written, dated decision at agent-os/specs/split-notifications-and-improvements/2026-05-06-unified-notifications-redesign/testing/test-plan.md:54 (2026-05-07): 'Do NOT mock IPusherService or vi.mock("pusher"). Let pusher.service.ts run end-to-end … Intercept those HTTP calls using MSW.' The same document states the general form at lines 54, 117, 206 and 222. It became doctrine on 2026-06-21 in d215a7fed (PR #3029, PURCO-3050), whose PR body generalises it - 'matching how the rest of the suite tests external edges' - with the checklist line 'No Stripe/email mocks remain in touched tests' and 182 injected mutations swept; 29 human comments and two CHANGES_REQUESTED rounds, none contesting the boundary. Archivist verdicts: intercept-at-the-wire deliberate/high; vi.mock module doubles accident/medium. Note the corrections manifest records that 'never spy on the publisher' was NEVER stated - the spec mandates a publisher spy at lines 400, 428, 441, 453 and 529 - so this rule bans mocking the transport and says nothing about spying. Adriana reported this aspect below-bar; that rested on a census column conflating vi.mock (9 files) with vi.spyOn (37). Corrected, the aspect clears at 119 of 120.

rules.statement: A test owns the data it exercises. It either creates the records it asserts on, or draws them from a named seed fixture module. A file that reads persisted rows back while doing neither is hunting the ambient seed, and is a violation.
rules.rationale: A test that hunts its subject out of the ambient seed makes the seed file its premise. A seed change then silently changes what is tested; a seed that no longer holds a matching row makes the test assert against null or skip its own body, passing while proving nothing; and any other test that mutates the found row makes this one flake. The file also cannot clean up what it does not own - 8 of the seed-reading files use afterEach against 107 of the 329 that create their own. The harness that once forced this is gone: getDbSingleton stands at zero occurrences, replaced by a per-test database in b364f5f90 (2025-11-06). Importing a NAMED seed fixture module counts as owning the data, because the test then depends on a declared, versioned population rather than on whatever the ambient seed happens to hold.
rules.archaeology: Verdict accident, high confidence. Seed reading entered in 8dba69395 (2025-09-30, PR #2289, PURCO-2510), where the first file named the shape in its own describe title, 'GetSenderAccountUseCase (integration, seeded DB)', pinning a hardcoded seed UUID and the literal expected value 'State Farm 2'. It was not chosen: the harness then was getDbSingleton, one shared database per run, so the seed was the only data there was. THE REVERSAL OUTRANKS THE INTRODUCTION: b364f5f90 (2025-11-06, PURCO-2575, PR #2397) deleted the TestDatabaseManager TRUNCATE helper and replaced the shared database with setup-db-per-test.ts, as a side effect of a performance change nobody reviewed. Since then 47 of 146 seed-reading files were converted across 26 unrelated feature commits, none saying why; 99 never moved; 6 went the other way. The only written position states side A - .claude/rules/testing-backend.md:11 (2026-07-16) - and was never enforced. VERSION 2 (2026-08-09): amended so a named seed fixture module counts as owning the data. VERSION 3: integrity note recording that Palmer entered a FABRICATED hash for the bucket-report fixture in version 2 without reading the file; the real hash is ef915dd1eeec969fdf4ef122f9a8e688b51fa95df4db860a41caec38057a0b33, and the append-only store cannot repair the bad row, which therefore reports drifted true and must be EXCLUDED from the acceptance gate. VERSION 4 (2026-08-09): detect corrected only, from a boolean that collected no sites to a real site collection. VERSION 5 (2026-08-09): appliesWhen and detect widened to admit the OrThrow read forms and raw-SQL reads, after both blind-gate Inspectors missed the same two fixtures for the same reason. VERSION 6 (2026-08-10): the checks were rewritten from raw text onto the AST vocabulary. Reads and creates are now matched as real call sites, the raw-SQL tags as identifiers in executable code, and the seed fixture modules as real import specifiers, so the word create inside a comment or a string can no longer excuse a file. All six labelled fixtures keep their verdicts and no backend file in the corpus changed verdict.

appliesWhen.human: The test file reads persisted rows back - it calls findFirst, findMany or findUnique in either form, or reads through raw SQL. A file that reads nothing back from the database is not applicable.

detect.human: Collect every read-back site, every creation site and every named seed fixture import in the file, with line numbers. The collection deliberately spans both sides so the inspector can pair each read-back with the creation that owns it, or show that none exists.

violates.human: Violation when the file reads persisted rows and neither creates any - no Prisma create, createMany or upsert call, and no raw SQL insert - nor imports a named seed fixture module. Seeding by raw SQL counts as creating, which is why the row-level-security suites pass. Importing a named seed fixture module counts as owning the data, which is why the bucket-report pattern passes. The create must be a real call site, not the word create inside a comment or a string.

rules.statement: No test or suite is left focused or parked in a committed file. `.only` is never committed. `.skip` and `.todo` are committed only when the title states why the test is parked.
rules.rationale: A parked test costs coverage that the suite still reports as green: the file passes, the count goes up, and the behaviour is unguarded with nothing in the run output saying so. `.only` costs more - Vitest runs that one test and silently drops every sibling in the file, so a green run can mean one assertion out of nineteen was executed. Nothing in this repository detects either: there is no eslint-plugin-vitest, no eslint-plugin-jest, and no CI grep over the vitest corpus, so the only barrier today is review. Captain Lasky ruled on 2026-08-09 that a skip whose title states the reason declares the gap rather than hiding it, and passes.
rules.archaeology: Verdict accident, high confidence: the 99.5% cleanliness is unenforced and nothing states the convention. No commit message, review thread or ticket anywhere records it, and greps of all three .eslintrc.js files for no-only, no-focused and no-disabled return nothing, as does a sweep of .github/workflows for a skip grep over the vitest corpus. The repository does author local ESLint rules for other things - eslint-local-rules/no-postgrid-writes.js and enums/no-magic-enum-strings.js - so writing one here was possible and was never done. The history separates two constructs the cluster merges: `.only` has NEVER been committed under src/server/** or src/utils/** in the repository's full history, with git log --all -S returning zero commits for it.only(, describe.only( and test.only(, while all three parked tests are `.skip` - create-payment.usecase.test.ts:829 in 2b5b8cead (2025-11-13, PR #2411) with no stated reason, review-payment.usecase.test.ts:498 in 44da2bb8d (2026-06-19, PURCO-3004) which writes its reason into the title, and a whole-suite describe.skip in convert-bmp-to-png.test.ts:44 from 6b75e44bf (2026-02-27, PURCO-2694).

appliesWhen.human: The test file declares at least one test of its own. The 25 generator shells delegate every test to file-usecase-test-suite.factory and declare none, so they can neither park a test nor follow the rule.

detect.human: Collect every focus or park modifier applied to a test declaration - it.only, it.skip, it.todo, test.only, test.skip, test.todo, describe.only, describe.skip, describe.todo - with its line number and the title string it carries. Do NOT collect runtime skips such as testCtx.skip(), and do NOT collect the word skip appearing as an object key or argument such as Prisma's skipDuplicates.

violates.human: Violation when the file commits any `.only`, or when it commits a `.skip` or `.todo` whose title does not state why the test is parked. A title that merely restates what the test would have asserted is not a reason. A title naming the missing guard, the blocking condition, or a ticket or pull request where the gap is recorded is a reason, and passes.

rubric.question: Is the matched modifier applied to a test declaration, rather than being a runtime skip such as testCtx.skip() or an object key such as skipDuplicates?

rules.statement: A test title states the behaviour in the present tense as a fact the subject performs - returns, throws, rejects, excludes. No title begins with "should".
rules.rationale: The title is what a failure prints in CI, and it is all a reader gets before opening the file. 'should throw error when X' does not say whether throwing is the expectation or the observation, so triage starts by opening the file; 'throws when X' names the behaviour that broke. The corpus already carries both vocabularies, so the same failure reads two different ways depending on which file it came from. This rule is advisory: a wrong title costs triage time, not correctness, and Captain Lasky judged on 2026-08-09 that blocking on 27 cosmetic findings is exactly the noise the near-total bar exists to prevent.

rules.statement: A test that claims to prove organisation isolation runs as a client contact, seeds or identifies a record owned by a DIFFERENT organisation, and asserts that record is absent from the result. An internal role is exempt from every organisation policy, so an isolation test with an internal actor proves nothing.
rules.rationale: Organisation scoping in this codebase is Postgres row-level security, not application filtering. A client contact is restricted to client_id = app_current_user_organization_id() on claims (db/security/claims/client-user-access.sql:9) and to organization_id = app_current_user_organization_id() on transactions (db/security/transactions/client-user-access.sql:10), and equivalently on payment_allocations, organizations, clients, claim_classifications, claim_classification_groups, custom_fields and mail_attachments. Internal roles bypass all of it through the blanket policy app_is_internal_user() (db/security/internal-user-policies.sql:15-17, 54-58), and createMockContext defaults the actor to SUPER_ADMIN. An isolation test written with the default actor therefore exercises no restriction whatsoever: it can pass while every organisation's rows leak. Cross-organisation leakage has recurred as a security defect in this application, so a test that appears to guard it while proving nothing is worse than no test, because it buys false assurance.
rules.archaeology: Drafted 2026-08-09 from a production trace plus a sweep of all 419 backend test files. The trace established that neither subject of the retired predecessor rule contains an actor-organisation branch at all: billing-account.repository.ts scopes by claim id then by the claim's client as billing-account owner, and get-payments-for-claim.usecase.ts derives its only session scope from getPortalPaymentSenderScope, which returns null unless the actor is an involved party, leaving claim_id plus type DEBIT. The predecessor, backend-authorization-cross-organisation-exclusion-proven, was retired for aiming at the wrong layer; it scored 2 of 5 and 1 of 5 in a blind gate and carried a detect check of ast:count(rawText(/organizationId/)) >= 0, true for every file. The sweep found 221 of 419 files read or seed an org-scoped table while only 101 mention a client-contact role, so 120 files touch organisation-scoped data exclusively as an exempt internal user. It also found tests that name isolation and cannot detect a leak: list-task.usecase.test.ts:2236-2296 carries a describe named cross-org isolation, an explicit SUPER_ADMIN actor at 2276, and two assertions at 2293-2294 of toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0), which hold for every possible result including a total leak, while seeding a real Org B claim and task so it reads as rigorous. get-actionable-count-task.usecase.test.ts:385 uses the same tautology. get-payments-for-claim.usecase.test.ts:1069-1094 and get-unallocated-payments-for-claim.usecase.test.ts:179-199 each carry three silent early returns that let the block pass with zero assertions executed. VERSION 2 (2026-08-09): appliesWhen widened before the rule was ever gated; nothing else changed and no fixture label moved. A mechanical pre-check of version 1 against its own five fixtures showed rls-enforcement.test.ts resolving to not-applicable although it is labelled follows and is the gold standard: the file never uses the words cross-org or isolation, describing itself as RLS enforcement on claims at line 26, so a title-keyed applicability check could not reach it. It drives the policy by hand instead, setting app.current_user_organization_id through set_config at line 140. Version 2 admits that session variable as an applicability marker, which brings the file into scope and lets it earn the pass its label requires. The widened check governs 44 backend test files. The same pre-check confirmed get-payments-for-claim.usecase.test.ts still resolves to pass mechanically while labelled violates: it carries no tautology token, and its fault is an internal default actor together with silent early returns at 1077, 1082 and 1088. That is deliberate and is why mechanization is partial rather than full - the check finds the tautology shape, and rubric q1 and q4 decide the actor and the silent-exit shapes.

appliesWhen.human: The test file declares a test whose title claims organisation isolation - cross-org, cross organisation, organisation or organization isolation, another or other organization, or the ISO marker used by the dashboard widget suites. A file that makes no such claim is not governed by this rule, however many organisations it touches; the rule polices the claim, not the coverage. A file is also governed when it sets or reads the row-level-security session variable app.current_user_organization_id directly, because a test that drives the policy by hand is making an isolation claim whether or not its titles say so.

detect.human: Collect, without judging: every role assigned to the acting session in the file, with its line - AuthorizationRoles members passed through createMockContext overrides, and any raw RLS session role; every assertion of absence, meaning toHaveLength(0), toEqual([]), not.toContain, rejects, or a comparison to null; every tautological assertion, meaning toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0) or toBeLessThanOrEqual on a length or count; and every silent exit, meaning a bare return or testCtx.skip() inside a test body.

violates.human: Violation when the file claims organisation isolation and its assertion cannot fail. Three shapes qualify. First, the acting role is internal - SUPER_ADMIN, ADMIN, SPECIALIST or CLIENT_DEVELOPMENT - because the blanket internal policy exempts it, so no organisation restriction is exercised. Second, the assertion is a tautology such as toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0), which holds for every result including a complete leak. Third, the block can exit through a bare return or testCtx.skip() when the seed lacks the shape it needs, reporting green having asserted nothing. A file that runs as a client contact and asserts a specific foreign-organisation row is absent passes. A file that uses an internal actor DELIBERATELY on a superuser non-RLS connection to prove a query's own organisation filter also passes, provided the title says so.

rules.statement: A test that names a retirement field - deletedAt, archivedAt or isArchived - either seeds a retired record and proves it is absent from a read, or, for a delete or archive subject, proves the record still EXISTS with the field set. Naming the field while seeding no retired record proves nothing, because the filter can be deleted and the test stays green.
rules.rationale: 47 models in this schema retire by flag rather than by row removal, and Claim carries a second axis in archivedAt. Every read path over them adds a deletedAt IS NULL predicate, so a test that never seeds a retired row exercises the predicate against a population where it can make no difference: remove the predicate from the repository and nothing fails. The delete side has the mirror hazard - asserting a row is gone would pass a hard delete, which is precisely the bug soft deletion exists to prevent, so a delete test must assert the row persists with the flag set.
rules.archaeology: Drafted 2026-08-09 from a sweep of the backend corpus. 219 files name deletedAt; 47 base models carry it, plus 24 shadow audit mirrors, and Claim adds archivedAt at schema.prisma:727 with its own restrictive policy. Followers exist on both sides. Exclusion: list-tags-for-management.usecase.test.ts seeds a deletedAt tag at 133 and asserts it absent at 141, and separately seeds an isArchived tag at 89 it asserts is KEPT at 110-113; list-claims-items.usecase.test.ts archives through archiveClaim at 4099 and asserts absence at 4102 with a total delta. Retired-not-removed: delete-saved-report.usecase.test.ts reads the row back with findUniqueOrThrow at 156-159 and asserts deletedAt equals a fixed instant. Violators: list-for-management.usecase.test.ts names deletedAt at 74 only to inspect already-returned rows and compares counts to a mirror Prisma query re-applying deletedAt null at 81, while never creating a soft-deleted user. Note the limit of this rule honestly: it cannot reach a test that ignores retirement entirely, which needs schema-aware applicability the check DSL cannot express. VERSION 2 (2026-08-10): the checks were rewritten from raw text onto the AST vocabulary and given the WHERE-clause escape. Seeding is now recognised by a retirement field passed into a create, update or upsert call, which catches the shorthand and parameter-passed forms the v1 literal regex missed; and a file whose only mention of a retirement field sits inside a where clause is no longer a violator, since that is a lookup on someone else's model. 108 backend files that v1 flagged now pass and one that v1 passed is now flagged; the six labelled fixtures all keep their verdicts, including the get-dashboard-config near-miss the v1 check got wrong.

appliesWhen.human: The test file names a retirement field or helper in executable code: deletedAt, archivedAt, isArchived, or archiveClaim. A file naming none of them is not governed - the rule polices a stated retirement concern, not every read of a soft-deleted model. This deliberately leaves a gap: a test whose subject filters deletedAt while the test never mentions it cannot be reached from the test file alone.

detect.human: Collect every site that SEEDS a retirement - a create or update setting deletedAt, archivedAt or isArchived, a call to archiveClaim or a delete usecase; every WHERE clause that merely filters on one of those fields; and every other mention of a retirement field. Return the sites, no verdict.

violates.human: Violation when the file names a retirement field but seeds no retired record and makes no persistence assertion - so the retirement filter under test could be deleted with every assertion still holding. Passing a retirement field into a create, update or upsert counts as seeding it, whatever the value is named. Inspecting deletedAt on rows the query already returned is not proof. A file passes when the only place it names a retirement field is a WHERE clause, because that is a lookup on someone else's model rather than a retirement concern of its own.

rubric.expects: Each field with its line, marked as a seed, an assertion, or an incidental lookup.

rubric.expects: The creation or archive line, or a statement that no retired record is ever created.

rubric.expects: The subject's model and whether the schema retires it by flag, or a statement that the field belongs to an unrelated query.

rubric.question: If the retirement predicate were deleted from the repository, would any assertion here fail?
rubric.expects: The discriminating assertion, or a statement that every assertion holds either way - including any mirror-query comparison that re-applies the predicate.

rules.statement: A test that establishes which tenant it runs as does so through the sanctioned tenant utility, never by spying on or mocking isPurCo/isSDI and never by stubbing the APPLICATION environment variables by hand.
rules.rationale: A spied tenant predicate makes the test prove the branch under a value the test invented, while production resolves the tenant from the environment; the two can diverge and the test stays green. The hand-stub is worse than redundant: setTenant() already stubs both APPLICATION and NEXT_PUBLIC_APPLICATION exactly as production reads them and resets between tests, and the successor utility useTenantEnvironment additionally deletes the OTHER tenant's seeded system user and internal organisation - because the seed plants both tenants' internal orgs into one test database. A test that only stubs the env var by hand therefore runs against a database still holding the other tenant's internal organisation and system user, so a query that must see one internal org sees two, and the test either asserts the wrong count or passes for the wrong reason.
rules.archaeology: Verdict deliberate, confidence high - the strongest evidence in the session. Origin ebd3dcd1e (2025-06-19, PR #2083), commit body 'retroactively remove ALL mocks for isPurCo'. The reviewer filed CHANGES_REQUESTED twice on that pull request: 'All the isPurCo mocks should be removed'. Six days earlier the same reviewer wrote the governing rule at 07f31bf64 (2025-06-13) in .cursor/rules/purco-testing.mdc: 'ALWAYS: Use setTenant() Utility - Never mock tenant utilities directly', explicitly banning vi.mock("~/utils/tenant-utils/is-purco") and vi.stubEnv("APPLICATION",...). The rule survives verbatim today at .claude/rules/testing.md:13. The ban was re-entered by the corpus from 2025-10-28 onward and is covered by no lint rule. A successor utility the written rule does not mention exists: tests/integration/utils/tenant-environment.util.ts exporting useTenantEnvironment (PR #3039), used by 2 files; Captain Lasky confirmed on 2026-08-09 that it is sanctioned. VERSION 1 PASSED THE BLIND ACCEPTANCE GATE on 2026-08-09, scoring 5 of 5 with both near-misses correct, on a sealed packet with fixtures and evidence stripped. VERSION 2 (2026-08-09): the detect check is corrected and nothing else changes. Version 1's detect was ast:count(rawText(/.../)) >= 0, which is true for every file and returns an empty sites array - every Inspector in the gate independently reported that it carries no information. Doctrine says detect must never return a verdict but must COLLECT sites; a boolean comparison collects nothing, so the Inspectors re-derived the sites by hand. The replacement is a plain grep over the same tokens, which returns the sites the rule speaks about. Captain Lasky ordered this fix across all eight affected rules on 2026-08-09, accepting that it returns this rule to unaccepted and requires a re-gate.

Naming the string 'PURCO' or 'SDI' is NOT applicability - the tenantStringLiteral column matches PURCO-XXXX ticket keys, the BILLING_ACCOUNT_TYPES domain enum and GOLDEN_PURCO_ROWS fixture names.

rules.statement: A test file that freezes the clock restores it. Any file calling vi.useFakeTimers or vi.setSystemTime also calls vi.useRealTimers.
rules.rationale: A frozen clock is process state, not file state. Vitest runs many files in one worker, so a clock left at a fixed instant is inherited by whatever runs next: date-dependent assertions in an unrelated file then compare against an instant nobody chose, and the failure surfaces in a file that never mentions time. Worse, it can pass - a due-date or age computation frozen at a convenient instant agrees with a wrong expected value, which is the exact silent shape this aspect exists to catch. The cost is paid at a distance from the cause, which is why 32 of the 33 freezing files already restore. This rule takes no position on whether a test should freeze the clock at all; that question is the clock-control contest and is decided separately.
rules.archaeology: Clock freezing is deliberate, high confidence. Fake timers became doctrine in a four-commit defect wave, every commit a filed date bug: PR #2530 (settled dates stored on the wrong day), PR #2534 (Mountain Time forms stored as the next UTC day, two review rounds and eight comments), PURCO-2655 via PR #2572 (committed date one day early on payment plans), and PURCO-3044 via PR #3023, which froze the workflow clock at FROZEN_NOW = 2025-08-15T12:00:00Z and drew three CHANGES_REQUESTED reviews from two reviewers. Two of the four are by an author who touched no other part of the idiom, in unrelated modules, within a fortnight - the spread signature of a shape that was taught. No reversal: the only commits removing the token delete or relocate whole files during restructures. Note that the restoration half of the idiom carries no separate argued origin; it is the near-unanimous companion practice, 32 of 33 files.

appliesWhen.human: The test file freezes the clock - it calls vi.useFakeTimers or vi.setSystemTime itself, or it calls an imported helper whose body does, such as anchorDenverClock. The helper is followed only when its name begins with a freezing verb - anchor, freeze, pin, lock, fake or stub - so a freezing helper named otherwise is invisible to the check and must be caught by the rubric.
